title: The real reasons US politicians are getting older
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: No country for young men and women: why do older politicians seem to have such a tight grip on the US political system?
content:
The real reasons US politicians are getting older

Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives.

The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump.

Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s.

Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states.

Hal Rogers, far left, with Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, centre, in 1996

The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed.

The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population.

At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it?

Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November.

Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters.

When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream.

The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans.

Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates.

Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website.

Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says.

The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56.

In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington

Mitch McConnell's recent long spell of absence has raised questions

But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively.

The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39.

There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too.

So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her.

Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too.

The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later, it had risen to 30%.

Pew adds that voters under 30 were underrepresented in 2024. Voters in that age category made up 20% of the voting-eligible population, though accounted for only 15% of all the votes that were actually cast.

Campaigners argue that these demographic trends matter because they leave some issues underrepresented.

"Yes, that might result in older people being elected, but I think it really skews, too, what issues are important; what issues politicians are incentivised to talk about and to take care of," says Grace Mausser, the co-chair of the New York City wing of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Zohran Mamdani has signposted a possible route for younger candidates

Mausser campaigned for Zohran Mamdani in his winning bid last year to become, at age 34, New York City's youngest mayor since 1892. Mamdani was held up as an example of a rare youthful success story, but his ally Mausser is less concerned with a politician's age than with their outlook.

Mausser says it is not necessarily a problem if someone has been in politics for a long time. Rather, the problem can be what may result from that: "You become so used to the language and the ideas of the political establishment that anything else - any new ideas, whether they come from young people or old people - seem crazy."

She invokes left-wing Democratic senator Bernie Sanders, 85, as an example of an older politician with a long tenure on Capitol Hill who has embraced change and had ideas that have resonated across generations.

In the US, older people hold politicians in far higher esteem than younger people - even more so than in many other countries, according to a Pew survey from spring 2025. Some 62% of 18-34-year-olds were likely to say few or none of their elected officials are honest, compared with 45% of people aged over 50. Of the 25 countries surveyed by Pew, only Greece's young adults had a more pessimistic view of the honesty of politicians.

For one expert who studies political engagement on both sides of the Atlantic, disaffection among young people helps to explain their unwillingness to participate in politics. The issue is not helped by the fact Congress has minimum age requirements for members, he says. Candidates must be 30 to serve as a senator, and 25 to be a representative.

"The one leads to another," remarks James Sloam from Royal Holloway, University of London. "If you don't have enough young people engaged in politics generally, then they won't become representatives."

What is more, Sloam says, young people in the US and the UK alike are alert to the fact that power does not just lie in politics. They are aware there are many other areas of work in which they can wield influence - including over elected officials.

Young voters tend to be less engaged than their older counterparts

For those young people who do end up in high-profile political positions, the next question is whether they can make a success of it, especially when it comes to parenthood. Over the summer, the stories of two high-profile young women working in Washington raised fresh questions around compatibility of the job with motherhood.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37, a Democratic congresswoman who took office aged 29, announced that she had started the process of freezing her eggs.

Later the same week in August, Karoline Leavitt, 29, who was appointed the youngest ever White House press secretary almost two years earlier, said she would leave the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her newborn baby. She explained: "I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of [being] the White House press secretary."

Only a handful of women have given birth while elected to Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18. The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave.

JD Vance, 42, one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, recently acknowledged that having young children might impact on his own decision to run for the White House in 2028, saying: "We've got four little kids."

America's two-party system is cited as another barrier to young people getting involved with politics.

Sloam, the London academic, says this is because only a relatively narrow range of views are represented. He highlights research that indicates young people are more energised by social movements or issue-based campaigns than by party politics.

And within party politics, he notes the example of Mamdani and others on the political left who appear to be galvanising youth support outside the Democratic Party mainstream. But he cautions that "it's a little bit sporadic at the moment".

The Republican Party has been through its own splintering over the last decade with the advent of Trump's MAGA movement, which appealed to a swathe of young men in the 2024 presidential election.

Some European democracies show a more pluralistic political environment can increase youth engagement, Sloam says. Scandinavian countries, for example, which are more likely to be multi-party, provide a clear counter example because the parties of government in those countries "work with those social movements to try and bring them into the political systems". Citing countries such as Norway, Sloam suggests there is a cycle whereby stronger youth turnout and youth trust in the political system leads to more involvement in politics.

It is true that some lawmakers should know when to call it a day, some experts argue, but equally, voters should not lose sight of the qualities of age. Nor should they confuse age with competency.

"Age alone is a very poor predictor of anything," says Tracey Gendron, a professor of gerontology at Virginia Commonwealth University whose research challenges the presumption that ageing is always linked to decline.

"You can have a 45-year-old who is experiencing depression or substance abuse who may not have the cognition necessary for the job," she says. And equally: "You can have an 85-year-old with incredible integrity and political judgement and wisdom who is fully capable of doing the job."

Gendron accepts the point that US politicians are not representative of the nation's age profile, but says this just shows that there are many ways in which Congress could afford to diversify.

"It's funny when we call it a gerontocracy and we focus just on age alone," she says. "When you look at most other aspects of representation - gender, sexuality, religion, race - we're not representative there either."

Democrat Maxine Waters' age has also been discussed

Owen, the Republican, fancies his chances in Utah, despite his opponent's much larger war chest.

Discussing what energises him as a Gen Z candidate, he identifies issues including the role of tech in public life, immigration and cost-of-living concerns. "I'm on the front end of starting my own family and looking at the costs and [asking] how am I going to make it work?" he says.

Asked if he sees any similarities between his campaign and the campaigns of young political candidates on the opposite side of the political spectrum, he says: "I'd break down the 'us versus them' framework, and maybe discard that a little bit… [there is] a bipartisan message that a lot of Americans on both sides of the aisle are feeling: that Washington isn't working for them."

He takes a similar view to Mausser, the democratic socialist in New York, that voters should not necessarily pick a candidate because they are young: what matters is their ideas.

"For me, it's much more about what you support, what you're who you're fighting for, than what year you were born," she says.

title: Chronic UTIs affect millions in the UK - these women are out to end the stigma
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Women are sharing their experiences with chronic urinary tract infections on social media in an effort to break the stigma surrounding UTIs.
content:
Adrianne says her chronic UTI has impacted her physically and mentally

"The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells her roughly 8,000 followers in a video on TikTok.

For nearly five years, Adrianne has lived with a chronic urinary tract infection (UTI) - a condition it took her two years to get a diagnosis for.

In that time she was wrongly told it was colon cancer, Crohn's disease or even that her partner must have been cheating and had given her a sexually transmitted infection.

What started as one UTI in 2022 became a debilitating cycle.

"It has completely stripped me of everything: being able to work properly, my relationships, my friendships, going out, being able to have a normal social life," says Adrianne, who works in digital marketing in London.

The 29-year-old was eventually diagnosed privately with a chronic UTI - something experts estimate could affect up to1.7 million women in the UK,external. Men and children are also affected.

Adrianne is not alone in sharing her story and coping mechanisms on social media to fight the stigma surrounding UTIs.

A quick search on Tiktok or Instagram shows hundreds of posts of women of all ages talking about the reality of living with recurrent and chronic UTIs.

"I felt incredibly nervous to put myself out there, but there's now this community of people who can share tips with each other, and understand each other," said Adrianne, saying her posts have had a "really positive response".

Like ‘weeing lava’: Living with chronic UTIs

A chronic UTI, which has no official medical definition, is an infection with persistent symptoms - even after a standard course of antibiotics. It can be caused by bacteria entering the lining of your bladder.

The condition can be unpredictable, but at its worst is "completely debilitating", says Adrianne, describing "the most excruciating abdominal pain, like shooting, spasming pain."

"You need a wee all the time, but it's like weeing lava."

"It's a very claustrophobic feeling, of I'm trapped in this body that is betraying me and is in pain," she adds.

Even on a good day she struggles to leave the house as she worries about having a flare-up.

While sending a urine sample to the lab remains the gold standard to diagnose a UTI, "false negatives" can often occur, says Professor Chris Harding, a consultant urologist at Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Another hurdle is the significant crossover between chronic UTIs and other conditions such as painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic pain and endometriosis, says Magda Kujawa, a consultant urologist at Stockport NHS Foundation Trust.

Adrianne says she felt "dismissed" by doctors while trying to get a diagnosis, and frustrated at repeatedly being given advice around hygiene and hydration, while her symptoms persisted.

Both experts say health professionals should listen to the patient's story to understand whether symptoms amount to a recurrent or chronic condition or something else entirely.

Since she started posting online, Adrianne has received messages from other young women who worry they are "dirty" and "not taking care of themselves" or that there is "something wrong with them".

"There's definitely still a lot of stigma around why people get them (UTIs), and it all just comes back to education. We're not taught about them at school," she adds.

Laura says not knowing when or how she would get better left her feeling "hopeless"

Laura Von Müllen, 26, has also been diagnosed with a chronic UTI and documents her experience on TikTok.

She says her symptoms "really badly" impacted university, and became particularly difficult to manage when she started working. She now works remotely from Kent doing social media management.

As well as urinary symptoms, Laura says she also experiences heart palpitations and panic attacks.

"People don't understand, they think it's just a UTI and that it'll clear within three days, but I've still got mine two years later," she says.

Laura also feels there is still a lot of misconception around UTIs. "People have said to me: who have you been sleeping with then? When that's not the case."

Adrianne and Laura hope more women sharing their experience will help demystify the condition.

Harding agrees. adding that "the more we can talk about these conditions, the more people will present to appropriate specialists and get the right treatment."

But both Harding and Kujawa warn that while social media can be a useful resource, there is the risk of coming across misinformation and harmful advice, including "hacks" that could cause more harm.

"I've seen women on social media sitting in baths of disinfectant, all because they were convinced that that they were dirty, and that's why they were getting infections. And actually, that just made things ten times worse," Kujawa says.

While Adrianne and Laura's symptoms are showing improvements, they say it's a "long road to recovery".

title: The Papers: 'Drill, Andy Drill!' and a Budget for 'bloody-minded entrepreneurs'
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Several of today's papers continue to follow the "storm" surrounding Andy Burnham's decision to approve a new gas field and what that will mean for future ones.
content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is "facing a storm" for approving drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which the Metro has headlined as "Drill, Andy, Drill!" The move has been praised by US President Donald Trump, the paper says, but not by those concerned about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh could reject a giant Rosebank oil field, sources have told the Guardian, after the approval of the Jackdaw gas field on Wednesday. According to officials, Fahnbulleh is considering "blocking what would be one of the biggest oil fields in the North Sea", the paper says.

"Pathetic" reads the Daily Mail headline about the Foreign Secretary Ed "Miliband's Net Zero madness" on potentially rejecting the Rosebank oil field. The Daily Mail calls Labour's approval of the Jackdaw gas field as a "rare outbreak of common sense".

The upcoming Budget will cut regulations and "back business in Britain making a profit", the chancellor has told the Times, in a move that will be for "bloody-minded entrepreneurs".

The Telegraph has been analysing Russian fishing vessels above critical UK undersea cables and suggests the Kremlin is using the fleet to "spy on Britain". The paper found "more than 500 incidents in which Russian trawlers loitered above vital communications cables".

Headteachers have spoken to the i Paper over fears their schools will have to find money for a national 3.5% teacher pay rise, "despite claims it would be 'fully funded'". The UK government has denied that the education secretary said the pay rise would be fully funded, the paper reports.

The Financial Times leads on the richest man in the world, Elon Musk, as he considers merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla into a "sprawling conglomerate spanning rockets, satellites, social media, robots and cars".  Investors are welcoming the idea, the paper reports, and shares in SpaceX surged on Wednesday.

"Britain must be ready" the Daily Express reports, amid growing threats of war. Senior Conservatives are urging Burnham to increase spending on defence to combat a rise in Russian threats, the paper says.

The Sun splashes on a picture of former Manchester City player Kyle Walker's "4 In A Row" leg tattoo that he said he will have removed if the club are stripped of its titles for breaching financial rules. The club was found guilty by an independent commission of more than 100 charges. City has denied any wrongdoing and has appealed the ruling.

The Prince of Wales faces off the Duke of Sussex on the front page of the Daily Mirror above the headline "Ruled Out". According to a royal insider, Prince William has "no intention" of engaging with Prince Harry, the paper reports, after the younger brother called for a reconciliation.

The Daily Star leads on TV personality and presenter Ryan Clark who said he "carpeted for missing work because of an air traffic strike" at the BBC.

And Donald Trump is the lead image on the Independent after he apparently "lashed out" at reporter Andrew Feinberg. The Independent reporter asked the president about fraud tip-off payments, which reportedly "triggered Trump".

The decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field is praised as"a welcome outbreak of common sense" in the Sun.,externalBut, in what is described as"Net Zero madness", the Daily Mail,externalsays the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is poised to reject plans for the Rosebank oil field. "Pathetic" is the paper's headline.A source tells the Times that it would be hard to justify,externalapproving the project on climate grounds. Another says Fahnbulleh has long been opposed to it. But, according tothe Guardian, she "could still be overruled",externalby the prime minister, who "may hear different representations" from the chancellor.

John Healey gives clues about next week'sBudget in an interview with the Times,external. He says that alleviating the cost of business is "in the end the only way to deal with people who have cost of living pressures". With the chancellor expected to cut regulations, a senior Treasury source likens them to "the sludge" which is "choking firms".

Separately, theFinancial Times reports that Healey has suffered a "double blow",externalwith increases in both inflation and government borrowing. One economist tells the paper the figures are "dismal" and signal that he will deliver a "cautious Budget that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal decisions for next year".

Analysis by the Daily Telegraph,externalsuggests that Russia is using fishing vessels to spy on the UK's undersea cables. The paper says these could be attacked in any future war, potentially paralysing the country. A Nato source is quoted as saying: "We're absolutely aware of what Russian civilian fishing ships are up to and where... Some of them have never seen a single fish on their deck." Meanwhile, warnings about Britain's readiness forwar are highlighted in the Daily Express,external, which calls for an increase in defence spending.

Anda royal insider tells the Daily Mirror,externalthat Prince William "has no intention of engaging with" his brother, Prince Harry, who has called for reconciliation. The source says "there isn't a world where the Prince of Wales can imagine" a reunion. The headline is: "Ruled out."

title: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Hotel chaos, transport mishaps and diplomatic blunders cast a spotlight on organisers and the firm hired to deliver the games.
content:
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.

There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".

Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.

"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.

The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.

Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.

Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to"stretch their legs out on the beds".

Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.

The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added,the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.

Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".

Container units were used to host some participants as organisers opted not to build a traditional athletes' village

This was just the start of the problems.

Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues andthe North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.

In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.

Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.

"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.

"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."

Organisers acknowledged major challenges and said athletes from some delegations had been inconvenienced

As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.

GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.

A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.

Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.

But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".

"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.

Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.

"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.

GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.

Volunteers were told they could attend the closing ceremony for free, before an organiser said that decision hadn't been approved

Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.

It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.

Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.

But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.

"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."

While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.

Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.

Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

title: Where did Britain’s missing “trillion pound” oil fund go?
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: For the first time, the Treasury calculates how much the UK could have raised by investing North Sea proceeds.
content:
The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea.

After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.

Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding housed in the National Wealth Fund.

A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.

It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?

It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time.

"The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said.

"If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."

On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.

The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's.

"Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.

It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.

Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences

It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.

The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.

Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.

The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.

I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.

Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.

It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.

While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.

UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.

Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.

Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?

title: Celebrity shark returns to South Korean canal despite efforts to guide it to sea
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Authorities had hoped the female shark would swim back to sea after being led out of the canal.
content:
Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canal

A famed dusky shark in South Korea has returned to the canal where she had been stuck for a month, just one day after authorities said they had successfully guided her out, local media report.

The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after she was spotted lingering in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.

South Korea's oceans ministry said on Wednesday evening they had led Bukangi out of the canal into an open harbour - but reports later said the shark had swum back to the mouth of the canal, having apparently broken through a barrier installed by authorities.

Another operation to relocate Bukangi has been scheduled for Thursday.

Authorities had attempted to lead the shark out of the canal

It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.

In the month that she has been in the canal, Bukangi has already attracted more than 1.6 million visitors.

Her popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.

But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as she appeared to be injured and was not eating. Social media users have been circulating videos of Bukangi swimming in the canal with what appears to be a bloodied snout.

There were concerns that she would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.

In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.

Hundreds of adoring fans cheered and waved goodbye to their shark, unaware that she would still be lingering in the canal by the next day.

Before Wednesday's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.

title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: The updated policy will apply to all reservations booked on the accommodation site on or after 20 November.
content:
Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to do

Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and  will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

title: Man Utd captain Fernandes rounds on boss Carrick after Champions League humiliation
author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
summary: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes blames head coach Michael Carrick for the tactics that led to an embarrassing 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League.
content:
Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on Carrick

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.

A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.

He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.

However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.

Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

Carrick 'angry' & Fernandes questions tactics - reaction to Man Utd's humiliating night

'That is on the manager' - Fernandes on Man Utd tactics

Carrick also refused to answer questions about his own future.

Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility.

"I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable.

"I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over.

"It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them.

"I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them.

"Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all."

Carrick responds to Fernandes criticism on tactics

After winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract.

However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland.

Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.

Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015.

Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time.

The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D.

It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent.

They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford.

Carrick 'bitterly disappointed' by Man Utd peformance

United flew straight back to Manchester after the game.

It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled.

Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada.

"There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch.

"It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times.

"I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can."

title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: The warning to US officials comes as at least three people die in the latest strikes at an airport and an oil field.
content:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis also attacked the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh earlier this month

The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.

Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.

The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.

Watch: Who are the Houthis, and why are they so hard to fight?

"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.

The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".

In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.

No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.

The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.

An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

title: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Test results have confirmed his diagnosis as a lung adenocarcinoma that was localised.
content:
Pope Leo returned to St Peter's Square on Wednesday for his weekly general audience

Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.

Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican.

"A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.

The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.

It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.

The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.

The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.

He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".

Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.

On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".

The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.

Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

title: Devon and Cornwall battening down the hatches ahead of Storm Austen
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are forecast to bring disruption across the South West.
content:
Staff at Perranporth's Watering Hole bar have secured parts of the building before Storm Austen

Extra safety measures have been set up by people and businesses as they prepare for the UK's first named storm of the season.

Storm Austen is forecast to bringgusts of up to 80mph (130km/h)and heavy rain across parts of Cornwall and Devon from Thursday night, according to the Met Office.

The conditions, which are also set to affect parts of Wales, England's south coast, Wiltshire and Somerset, have led totwo weather warnings being issued,externalfor Friday.

Bosses at The Watering Hole bar on Perranporth Beach in Cornwall said they were taking extra precautions after the venue suffered damage duringStorm Gorettiin January.

Jamie-Lee Job said the bar lost several glass panels during that storm as the wind physically lifted them up and sent them crashing through a roof canopy.

Ahead of Storm Austen, staff at the bar have been fixing parts of the building down to make them more secure.

"It was quite scary, we've survived a lot of storms but that particular storm we underestimated how bad it was going to be," Job said.

"It is a reminder to us all to best err on the side of caution.

"So for this one we are doing everything we can do to make sure everything is secure and hopefully the roof stays on for this one."

Jamie-Lee Job said The Watering Hole lost a lot of glass panelling during Storm Goretti in January

The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind on Friday from 00:00 until 14:00 BST. It covers Devon, Cornwall, south Wales, England's south coast, Wiltshire and Somerset, with "transport disruption likely and possible damaging winds in some areas".

From 03:00 until 10:00 this warning is increased to amber for Cornwall, with power cuts and building damage listed among possible consequences.

TheMet Office is advising people,externalto make preparations to protect their property and other people from injury.

It recommends checking for loose items outside homes and making plans to secure them, including bins, garden furniture, trampolines, tents, sheds and fences.

The Watering Hole was badly damaged by a storm in January

Other people in Perranporth said they had stocked up on supplies in case they lost power during Storm Austen.

Chris Eves said: "We've got loads of torches and candles and lots of flasks so we should be OK."

Another woman who was walking along the town's beach said she was preparing to "hunker down".

She added: "I've got lots of candles, we've got a rechargeable radio, rechargeable lights, a gas-fired pizza oven and I am thinking about buying a primus stove as well.

"I am also thinking I won't have anything expensive in my freezer, so if there's a power cut I won't lose too much."

Cornwall Council has issued a warning urging people to prepare before the storm hits and to avoid exposed coastal areas on Thursday evening and Friday.

"Strong winds and large waves could make conditions extremely dangerous," the council said.

Camborne Rugby Club said it would be closing its club grounds for at least 24 hours from 15:00 on Thursday, while its clubhouse would be shut from about 22:00.

Josie Tennant said the Pebbleridge Kitchen in Devon had a plan in place for the high winds

In Devon, storm preparation at the Pebbleridge Kitchen near Northern Burrows Country Park is a "well-versed process" after the last winter.

Josie Tennant, operations manager across the Royal George Group, which runs the cafe, said: "We're super exposed here so we make sure all the furniture is against the building so that anything moving around is not moving too far so it can't hurt anyone.

"We also make sure all the shutters are down so the rain is not being driven into the building and then we are looking out for red alerts as well."

She added: "The manager Sam here knows exactly what to do to keep the building safe to keep the staff safe and to keep our customers safe as well."

RNLI Coxswain Simon McCarthy said his crew was ready to go out at any time

The RNLI has reminded those along the coast to exercise "extreme caution if visiting the shoreline, especially along exposed cliffs and seafronts".

Appledore RNLI Coxswain Simon McCarthy said his crew was ready to go out "at any time" and was securing its boats withextra lashings while monitoring the storm.

"With the amber warning, it means the all-weather lifeboats are more called upon," McCarthy explained.

"The inshore boats have got their limitations, so we have to make sure we have crew available."

He added: "We really do want people to be sensible. The sea will always win."

Devon County Council said it would have extra staff on hand in its Network Operations Control Centre to monitor conditions and co-ordinate responses to any weather-related incidents.

Councillor Dan Thomas, cabinet member for highways, said: "We're preparing for a spell of unsettled weather and would encourage everyone travelling around Devon to keep an eye on the forecast and plan ahead.

"With many trees still in leaf following the dry weather, there is a risk of fallen trees and branches on our roads."

Dartmouth Food Festival has also been impacted by the storm with organisers pushing some events planned for Friday back to Saturday morning.

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
summary: Moscow says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
content:
Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities

Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.

Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.

The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.

Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."

The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.

Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace

Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.

It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.

Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".

Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.

Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St Petersburg

Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."

Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".

Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.

"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.

Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"

Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."

The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.

Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".

That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.

Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.

Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", andZelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".

Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.

US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisangroup of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.

Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for Ukraine

Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.

Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.

When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.

"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

title: Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50
author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
summary: Why England Rugby World Cup winner Phil Vickery has started entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50.
content:
Vickery's journey from Rugby World Cup winner to bodybuilder

It could have been deep in the bowels of English rugby's national stadium in Twickenham.

Instead, Phil Vickery was backstage at the Physical Culture Show in Hull, waiting for his moment - but this time as a bodybuilder.

"It reminded me of being in the changing room before the big game, your nerves - are you going to be sick, you're happy, you're not happy, I can do this, this is raw," he said, adding that just recalling that moment earlier this month makes his hair stand on end.

"That nervous energy and waiting and then, oh, it's just a horrific feeling. All the girls and boys can relate to that, because that's the same at whatever level of sport you play.

"I'm questioning myself, should I even be there? But then you go, actually, do you know what? I've done the work. I've done the graft."

What started as an ambition to get fit has ignited a passion for mental and physical fitness, and for Vickery being the best version of himself.

It's 23 years since Phil Vickery was part of the England team that won the Rugby World Cup final in Australia

Then came a challenge from his friend Lee Powell and, with support from his physical trainer Dave Campbell, Vickery entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50. Posing to the strains of the familiar World Cup anthem World in Union.

"What it probably did for me is ignite that ex-pro rugby player in me of detail, discipline, turning up when it's dark and dingy and cold, competing, and we went from there," Vickery said.

"What I've fallen in love with, with the bodybuilding, it's a very singular, isolated sport, because it is you against you. It's not about anyone else.

"There is no out. You can't hide behind a keyboard. You are stood on stage. Your physique and what you look like is a direct reflection of your effort and what you have done, and that is quite scary."

The former Gloucester and Wasps prop won 73 caps for England, five more for the British and Irish Lions.

Victory at the 2003 Rugby World Cup in Australia was a sporting zenith in a career that includes being a businessman and a Celebrity MasterChef winner.

But personal struggles and a diagnosis for probable CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy), for which Vickery is part of acontinuing litigation battle,means he has had to manage his mental health.

"We all deal with things differently," he said. "I think having the gym and having that space to be able to work is really important for my mental health, but also for my body physically, because it is broken, so I use it in that sense.

"I think the one thing I really struggled with when I finished playing is I trained to play and I couldn't find that reason to train afterwards.

"And although you should train for yourself or your wellbeing, it probably took a low point or something to actually trigger it.

"But, probably, the bodybuilding - or doing the show or doing the original transformation - I have to close the circle. You know, you have a plan, you make a plan, you implement it, you commit to it, see it through, and then it's over and it's done. And then you move on."

Vickery won 73 caps for England and five for the British and Irish Lions as a prop forward

When Vickery took to the stage in Hull, he says he weighed about 99kg. More defined, but lighter than his playing days when he said his weight would range between 118kg and 135kg.

"[On stage] you look the best version of you that you could look, but you feel the worst. It's kind of a silly sport but it's amazing what the human body can do.

"Age, for me, doesn't bother me at all. I still think I'm 27. My body tells me different."

Training now involves three or four weight sessions a week, combined with daily walks (fasting cardio) and a protein-rich diet.

He hopes more shows will follow in the future.

"I can't do what I used to do and I think the battle for me, certainly when I finished [playing] and even to this day, is you cannot get back those feelings that you had when you used to do what you do," he said.

"I think doing things which can get you outside, test you physically and mentally, and put you in those uncomfortable positions. It's repurposing the skills that you've learned. You've just got to use them in a different way.

Vickery is known for his openness. He posts regularly on his social media channels about his health and fitness. But he's not comfortable with being labelled as an "influencer".

"I don't think everyone should go bodybuilding. My message is trying to be positive. Get out, do something, make a plan."

"I know I will never be a top bodybuilder. But it doesn't stop me, it doesn't stop me having a go and being the best version of me that I can be."

title: Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation
author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
summary: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes blames head coach Michael Carrick for the tactics that led to an embarrassing 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League.
content:
Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on Carrick

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.

A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.

He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.

However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.

Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

Carrick 'angry' & Fernandes questions tactics - reaction to Man Utd's humiliating night

'That is on the manager' - Fernandes on Man Utd tactics

Carrick also refused to answer questions about his own future.

Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility.

"I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable.

"I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over.

"It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them.

"I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them.

"Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all."

Carrick responds to Fernandes criticism on tactics

After winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract.

However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland.

Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.

Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015.

Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time.

The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D.

It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent.

They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford.

Carrick 'bitterly disappointed' by Man Utd peformance

United flew straight back to Manchester after the game.

It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled.

Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada.

"There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch.

"It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times.

"I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can."

title: Goal, assist... goal-kick - Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials
author: https://www.facebook.com/BBCSport/
summary: Why Declan Rice backs his England team-mate Harry Kane to win the Ballon d'Or after Arsenal's draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League.
content:
Is it 'phenomenal' Kane's year to lift the Ballon d'Or?

Even by Harry Kane's remarkable standards, this was mightily impressive.

There were fewer than 25 minutes on the clock during Bayern Munich's thrilling 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League when the forward took matters into his own hands in a bid to break the deadlock.

As the Premier League champions prepared to defend a Bayern goal-kick, Kane seized the initiative by launching his side up the pitch with a raking 80-yard pass.

It was a moment of remarkable ingenuity from the England international, one that almost ended with Bayern taking the lead.

"Under Vincent Kompany, he has been given a level of trust that he has probably never had before under any other manager," former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport.

"For all the things we've seen him do and the positions we've seen him roam into, nobody has seen him take a goal-kick before.

"But even someone like Manuel Neuer, who is his senior and has been at Bayern for a large part of his career, sees Harry Kane put the ball down and thinks, 'OK, sure'. He lets Harry go for it because he thinks whatever he sees is going to be correct.

"At the same time, there were Bayern players running forward because they knew that the ball could come.

"For him to be taking a goal-kick is not something you may want to see very often. You don't necessarily want your number nine to be THAT deep, but the nature of his game when he is playing for Bayern is to roam, and today it was a huge benefit to the team."

Although Kane was denied the opportunity to add another outstanding assist to his already impressive catalogue, he did not have to wait long to make another decisive contribution.

After Eberechi Eze had put Arsenal ahead, Kane helped Bayern restore parity, bending a sumptuous pass around Jurrien Timber for Alphonso Davies to finish.

The England captain then fired the hosts in front from the penalty spot midway through the second half, taking his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16.

But Declan Rice struck late on to earn Arsenal a share of the spoils.

Kane recorded 40 touches in Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Arsenal

For Kane, it was another mesmerising performance that underlined his credentials as the frontrunner for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

The former Tottenham Hotspur captain, 33, could become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the prestigious individual award, with Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Paris St-Germain forward and current holder Ousmane Dembele among the favourites.

Kane was named on the 30-man shortlist in September, with the winner due to be announced on Monday following a vote by an international jury of 100 journalists.

"He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves. The year he has had has been remarkable," Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice told TNT Sports.

"When you play with him, you realise how good he is, and when you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is.

"He is ridiculous, such a good player, and I am lucky I can play with him, not so lucky I have to play against him."

By scoring against Arsenal on Wednesday night, Kane became only the second player in Champions League history to find the net in 10 consecutive matches.

The only other player to achieve the feat was five-time Ballon d'Or winner Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 successive matches for Real Madrid between June 2017 and April 2018.

"Kane certainly looks at home at Bayern. He understands the team and its system, and they all understand him. They know that when he gets the ball at his feet, wherever that may be, something good can happen," Onuoha added.

"I think all the Bayern players are really playing into that, but then Harry steps up and scores a penalty as well.

"Having freedom is probably the best way to describe what he has got playing for Bayern, because he will work hard defensively, which allows him the freedom to be creative when he is in attack. For now, he certainly is thriving."

Kane's goal against Arsenal took his tally to 156 in 158 appearances since joining Bayern Munich from Tottenham in 2023.

It was another night to remember for the England captain, but the best could yet be to come, with the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London looming.

"It would be amazing to win," said Kane afterwards. "The voting closed a long time ago so there's nothing I can do, just wait and see what happens."
